doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Slow arranging, Spinning Wheel, and Lew Soloff's memorial
summary: He wrote Spinning Wheel in an afternoon, and played Folk Song with Randy Brecker at Soloff's memorial.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: But getting back to Lew. I was a slow arranger so a couple, I’m not going to mention any people, but I did maybe one-third of the charts. Dick was very quick. And three or four of the charts like I couldn’t finish. I got very emotional because I didn’t have a technique like Dick was talking about you know. He had to write for strings for the week. His assignment, or a choral thing, you know, voices. And I didn’t have to do that at Berklee, maybe once or twice so I didn’t get over that. So I was very slow usually. “Spinning Wheel” was written in one afternoon. That’s crazy. And I told my wife, whose favorite band was Blood, Sweat & Tears and she’s from Japan. And I said I wrote that in one afternoon. I wasn’t bragging I just said I usually take a month like Bobby Brookmeyer or someone I’ve heard is very slow but he writes great. So if it takes me that long it takes me that long you know. But the thing about Lew, and I played at his memorial with Randy Brecker, I played a tune that he loved, a ballad called “Folk Song” that I wrote when I was 17, 18 years old. A slow piece. He loved it but he never recorded it. And I was going to play “Over the Rainbow” solo piano for his memorial a few years ago and I found out that no one else was playing solo. You know the Gil Evans band and actually Lew’s ex- wife played harp. But I didn’t know that. And so I was getting names of people that were

going to perform. I thought it’d be an ego trip, I’m the one guy coming from Boston down to the New York area, everybody else, there’s about fifteen musicians, Wynton Marsalis played also. But most people came from New York. And when they asked me to play, Noah Evans who was in charge of recruiting people, and Steve Shaffer. Is it Steve?

Paul Shaffer. They were getting people. So the first group of people on the list in an email, and I’m thinking I’d like to play “Over the Rainbow” because I’ve played it and it really opens people’s hearts with my reharm and the way I play it. But I don’t want to show off and being the only guy that’s — you know I’m coming down and I’m just going to play by myself. They asked me to play with the band. And I have hearing loss so I didn’t want to play with anybody, loud music. I don’t care how good they play I just don’t want to hurt my ears anymore. I want to hear the birds still. Because I have some serious hearing loss in the high range. But then there was another list a week later as they were getting this list together and I said, Randy, I said let me do something with Randy. Maybe “Over the Rainbow” with my reharm I sent him, and this tune “Folk Song.” So Randy said, “Let’s do ‘Folk Song.’” So we did that. Lew — we were pretty close. But honestly when I’ve been with Lew at some clubs, like I was mentioning before the interview, when I went down to New York one of the last times I played with him I sat in. I asked if I could play. He was playing in a jazz club, only a few people there. But outside the club I’m there with a friend of mine and he was telling other people, he said, “Fred’s the guy.” The false — I take it but Dick Halligan was a great arranger, David Clayton Thomas to me was the best pop singer, he had the strongest voice. He could sing any kind of music. I love Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder, Stevie Winwood, but David could sing any kind of music you know.
